title: Mirror Stance Hold
instructions: Stand facing a full-length mirror with feet shoulder-width apart.
Step your lead foot forward and your rear foot back about one shoulder-width, rear foot turned out roughly 45 degrees.
Bend your knees slightly and settle your weight onto the balls of both feet, posture tall.
Raise your hands to guard and hold the position for 60 seconds without shifting your feet.
Check the mirror: hips and shoulders half-turned to the target, not fully square and not fully sideways.
Rest 30 seconds and repeat for 3 holds, resetting your feet from scratch each time.
coaching_points: Tall spine, chin tucked, eyes level — don't crouch to feel stable
Weight balanced and ready to move either direction, not planted
Breathe normally; tension in the shoulders means you're forcing it

title: Tape Line Stance Reset
instructions: Lay two strips of tape on the floor, parallel, about shoulder-width apart.
Start in your stance with each foot on its line.
Step-drag forward three steps, keeping each foot tracking along its own line.
Step-drag back to the start, then step-drag laterally left and right the same way.
After every direction change, freeze and check: feet back on the lines, stance width unchanged.
Work for 3 minutes, resetting to the taped stance whenever your feet drift.
coaching_points: The step-drag keeps your base identical after every move
If your feet leave the lines, your steps are too big
Finish every movement in a stance you could punch from

title: Partner Balance Push Test
instructions: Take your boxing stance; a partner stands in front of you.
The partner gives your lead shoulder a firm, slow push — a steady press, not a shove.
Absorb it without stepping, hopping, or straightening your legs.
Repeat with pushes to the rear shoulder and to each side.
If you lose balance, adjust your stance (usually: sink lower, weight centered) and try again.
Do 30 seconds of pushes from each of the four directions.
coaching_points: A good stance absorbs pressure; a bad one topples or bounces
Knees stay soft and springy, never locked
If you consistently fall forward, your weight is too far over your lead foot

title: Slow 1-2 Stance Check
instructions: Face a partner or mirror in your stance.
Throw a slow jab-cross at half speed, then freeze fully at the end of the cross.
Check your feet: same stance width and angles as before the punches, weight centered.
Return to guard slowly, then repeat — 10 reps, then switch to a slow 1-2-3.
Have the partner call out any foot that lifted, slid, or turned during the punches.
Finish with 1 minute of continuous slow 1-2s, freezing at random on the partner's clap.
coaching_points: Punches should not move your foundation; power comes through it, not from leaving it
Rear foot pivots on the cross but stays grounded — no lifting
If your stance widens every combo, you're pushing off instead of rotating

title: Three-Minute Stance Discipline
instructions: Set a timer for one 3-minute round and take your stance.
Every 30 seconds, throw a crisp 1-2-3 combination and immediately reset to your exact starting stance.
Between combinations, make small step-drag adjustments only — never stand up or widen out to rest.
In the final minute, add pivots after each combination while keeping the stance intact.
When the round ends, note when your legs wanted to quit: that's the habit to train out.
Build to 3 full rounds with 1-minute rests.
coaching_points: Fatigue reveals stance flaws — this drill trains the stance to survive them
Rest by narrowing slightly and breathing, never by standing tall
Your guard and stance are one system; both must last the round

title: Jab Snap-Back in the Mirror
instructions: Face a mirror in your stance at jab range from your reflection.
Throw a slow, full-extension jab, watching your lead hand travel straight out and back.
Snap the hand back along the exact same path to your cheek — as fast as it went out.
Freeze for one beat with the glove touching your cheekbone and check: rear hand never moved.
Repeat for 2 minutes, then do 1 minute where every third jab is a double jab, both hands returning cleanly.
Finish with 30 seconds of full-speed jabs, guard return still instant.
coaching_points: The punch is only half the technique; the return is the other half
A lazy return after the jab is the most common way beginners get countered
Elbow stays tucked on the return, not flared out

title: Tennis Ball Chin Shadowboxing
instructions: Tuck a tennis ball (or rolled-up sock) under your chin, holding it against your chest with your jaw.
Shadowbox for 2 minutes: jabs, crosses, hooks, footwork — everything.
If the ball drops, stop, reset it, and continue; count your drops.
Round two: add head movement — slips and rolls — without losing the ball.
Goal is zero drops by the third session, not the first.
Finish with 1 minute of fast combinations, chin still pinned down.
coaching_points: Chin down, eyes up — you watch the opponent over your guard, not from under it
A lifting chin when punching is a knockout invitation
Keep the jaw relaxed; clenching the ball creates shoulder tension

title: Freeze Guard Check
instructions: Shadowbox freely while a partner watches (or set a timer to beep every 20 seconds).
On the call or beep, freeze instantly — mid-punch, mid-step, wherever you are.
Check three things: knuckles at cheekbone height, elbows touching your ribs, chin tucked.
Score yourself: 3/3 is a pass; anything less, do 10 push-ups and continue.
Work for 3 minutes; the freezes should catch you in honest positions, not posed ones.
Advanced version: partner calls freeze only right after your combinations, when guards sag most.
coaching_points: Your guard at the freeze is your real guard — the rest is wishful thinking
Elbows protect the body; flared elbows open the ribs and telegraph fatigue
Gloves cover the chin, not the eyes — you must see through your guard

title: Towel Pin Elbow Drill
instructions: Fold a small towel and wedge it between your rear upper arm and your ribs.
Throw slow crosses for 2 minutes without letting the towel fall.
The cross must come from hip and shoulder rotation — if your elbow wings out, the towel drops.
Switch the towel to the lead side and throw slow lead hooks the same way.
Final minute: alternate cross and lead hook, towel pinned on each side in turn.
When you can do 3 minutes clean, the elbow discipline is becoming automatic.
coaching_points: Elbows-out on the cross bleeds power and opens your body
Rotate the torso to deliver the punch, don't reach with the arm
Rear hand returns to the cheek every time — the towel only tests the elbow

title: Shell Coverage Under Taps
instructions: Take a high guard: gloves at temples/forehead, elbows tight to the body, chin tucked.
A partner wearing gloves taps lightly at your guard — head, sides, body — for 60 seconds.
Don't punch back; just maintain the shell, keep your eyes open, and breathe.
Between taps, the partner occasionally pauses — don't drop your hands in the pause.
Rest 30 seconds and repeat for 4 rounds, with the partner varying speed and angle.
Final round: you may step and pivot while shelling, but the coverage never opens.
coaching_points: Eyes open and breathing — beginners hold their breath and look away
A tight shell is forearms and gloves, not hunched shoulders
The pause is the test: tired fighters drop their hands the moment pressure stops

title: Guard Integrity Footwork Round
instructions: Set a 3-minute timer. You'll move continuously — no punching in this drill.
Step-drag forward, back, and laterally; add pivots and direction changes on your own rhythm.
Your gloves do not leave your cheekbones for the entire round — not during pivots, not during quick steps.
A partner randomly calls single punches ('jab!', 'hook!'); mime the block or parry and snap straight back to guard.
If a glove drops below chin level at any point, restart the round.
Build to 3 consecutive clean rounds.
coaching_points: Footwork and guard are trained together because they fail together
Fast feet make hands lazy — this drill breaks that link
The mime-block must be small; big defensive motions open bigger holes

title: Wall Jab Range Finder
instructions: Stand facing a wall at full arm's length plus one fist — mark the spot with tape.
Throw slow jabs at a small target on the wall (a taped X at chin height).
The jab must land with a fully extended arm while your torso stays upright — no leaning in.
If you can't reach without leaning, you're too far: adjust your starting distance, not your posture.
Do 3 minutes of slow jabs, then 1 minute stepping in with the jab and stepping back out.
Your head should finish every jab exactly where it started.
coaching_points: Overreaching shifts your weight past your lead foot and kills your balance
The shoulder extends to deliver the jab; the spine stays stacked
Judge distance with the jab — it's your measuring stick, not a lunge

title: Step-In Jab Timing
instructions: Start in your stance, well out of jab range from a heavy bag or wall target.
Step-drag forward and let the jab land at the exact moment your lead foot plants.
Step back out to your starting spot; reset fully.
Repeat for 2 minutes slow, focusing on the foot-hand landing sync.
Next 2 minutes: vary it — sometimes step in without punching (feint the entry), sometimes double up the jab on the step.
The punch and the step are one movement, not two stacked together.
coaching_points: Landing the punch as the foot plants puts your body weight behind it
Stepping then punching is late; punching then stepping is a reach — sync them
Keep the rear hand glued to your cheek through the entire entry

title: Cross Pivot Freeze in the Mirror
instructions: Face a mirror in your stance.
Throw a slow cross: pivot the rear foot, rotate the hips, then the shoulders, arm extending last.
Freeze at full extension for 2 seconds and check the mirror: rear heel turned, hips and shoulders rotated, chin behind the lead shoulder.
Slowly retract along the same path; rear hand returns to the cheek.
Do 10 slow reps, then 1 minute of continuous slow crosses with a freeze every fifth one.
Finish with 30 seconds at moderate speed — the rotation pattern must survive the speed.
coaching_points: Power travels ground to fist: foot pivot, hip turn, shoulder turn, then arm
An arm-only cross is a push — rotation is what makes it a punch
The chin stays down through the whole rotation; lifting it is the classic cross mistake

title: Lead Hook Geometry
instructions: Face a mirror in your stance, lead side toward the mirror.
Throw a slow lead hook: pivot the lead foot, rotate the hips, arm bent at roughly 90 degrees.
Freeze at the contact point — check: elbow level with the fist, shoulder touching your chin, rear glove still on your cheek.
The punch travels on a tight arc, ending in front of your own chin line — never swung wide past it.
Do 10 slow reps, then 2 minutes of slow hooks with full freezes.
If your elbow drops below your fist, shorten the arc until the 90-degree bend holds.
coaching_points: A 90-degree elbow keeps the hook short, fast, and structurally strong
The lead shoulder ends at the chin — it becomes part of your guard
Wide looping hooks are slow and visible; tight hooks land first

title: Dip-and-Drive Uppercut
instructions: Stand in your stance in front of a mirror or bag.
Bend your knees 3-4 inches — a small dip, not a squat — keeping your back straight and chin down.
Drive upward: legs extend, hips rotate, and the punch travels straight up the center line, palm facing up.
The power comes from the leg drive and rotation; the arm just delivers it.
Freeze at the top: fist at chin height of an imaginary opponent, elbow still bent, other hand on your cheek.
Do 3 x 1-minute rounds alternating lead and rear uppercuts, slow first round, moderate after.
coaching_points: No dip, no uppercut — arm-only uppercuts have nothing behind them
Keep the punch tight to your center; wide uppercuts miss and expose you
Don't drop the punching hand before throwing — that's a telegraph, not a wind-up

title: 1-2 Freeze Balance Check
instructions: In your stance, throw a 1-2 at half speed and freeze with the cross fully extended.
Hold 2 seconds and audit: weight centered between the feet, head behind the lead shoulder, rear foot pivoted but grounded.
Slowly return to stance; repeat 10 times.
Next round: have a partner watch for telegraphs — shoulder dips, hand pulls, weight shifts before the punches.
Eliminate one telegraph at a time: the 1-2 should look identical to your guard until the punches fire.
Finish with 1 minute of continuous 1-2s at moderate speed, freezing on a random clap.
coaching_points: If you're off balance at the freeze, the punches were thrown with a lunge, not rotation
Telegraphs are habits, not necessities — film yourself if no partner is available
Every punch starts and ends in the same stance; the stance is home base

title: Hook Off the Jab (Heavy Bag)
instructions: Work the heavy bag at jab range for a 3-minute round.
Every combination starts with a jab; the lead hook follows it — jab-hook, jab-jab-hook.
The hook must pivot the lead foot and rotate the hips — no arm swings.
After each hook, the hand snaps back to the cheek before anything else happens.
Round two: add the cross between them — jab-cross-hook — keeping the same hip rotation on every punch.
Count clean hooks per round; raise the count each session without losing form.
coaching_points: The jab occupies the guard; the hook exploits the opening it creates
Hook power is hip rotation, not arm speed — pivot hard on the lead foot
Return the hook to the cheek fast; the follow-through is where counters land

title: Single-Punch Power Ladder
instructions: Face the heavy bag in your stance.
Throw ONE jab with full technique — step, rotation, snap — then fully reset to stance.
Throw ONE cross with full rotation and pivot, then reset.
Continue through lead hook, rear hook, lead uppercut, rear uppercut: 10 perfect singles each.
Rest 1 minute, then repeat the ladder at slightly higher speed — technique must not decay.
If a punch feels weak, slow down: this drill rewards mechanics, not output.
coaching_points: Isolating single punches exposes which ones are arm punches in disguise
The full reset between punches builds the habit of returning to stance
Power is technique expressed fast — earn the speed with clean slow reps first

title: Double-End Bag Timing
instructions: Work the double-end bag for 3-minute rounds.
Punch the bag as it rebounds toward you — meet it, don't chase it.
Focus on snap: fist out and back in a blink, faster than the bag's return.
Throw only when the timing is right; waiting for the moment is part of the drill.
Add slips: after each combination, slip the imaginary counter as the bag comes back.
Build from 2 rounds to 4 as your timing sharpens.
coaching_points: The double-end bag punishes pushing — only snapped punches control it
Timing beats speed; a well-timed punch lands while a fast wild one misses
Keep your eyes on the bag through the whole exchange, especially while slipping

title: Step-Drag in Four Directions
instructions: Take your stance in the center of your space.
Move forward: step with the lead foot first, then drag the rear foot up to restore stance width.
Move back: step with the rear foot first, then drag the lead foot.
Move left: lead foot steps, rear foot follows. Move right: rear foot steps, lead foot follows.
Work each direction for 1 minute, then 2 minutes mixing directions on your own call.
Never cross your feet, never let them touch — the stance survives every step.
coaching_points: The foot nearest the direction of travel always moves first
Small steps keep you ready to punch; big steps leave you stranded
Stay on the balls of your feet — flat feet can't step-drag

title: Pivot Clock Drill
instructions: Imagine a clock face on the floor; you start at 6 o'clock facing 12.
Pivot 45 degrees on your lead foot, letting the rear foot swing around — land balanced, guard up.
Work through 90 and 180 degrees, then repeat pivoting the other direction.
After each pivot, freeze: you should be able to throw a clean 1-2 immediately.
Do 2 minutes of pivots on call (partner calls the angle), then 2 minutes freestyle.
Small pivots for small angles; keep the lead foot as the anchor every time.
coaching_points: Pivot on the ball of the lead foot, not the heel
The pivot creates a new angle while keeping you in punching range
Head stays level through the turn — bobbing up gives away the move

title: Lateral Line Shuffle
instructions: Lay a straight line of tape about 15 feet long on the floor.
Shuffle laterally along the line: 10 steps one way, 10 back, staying low.
Your feet never cross and never click together — push off the inside edge of the trailing foot.
Keep your guard up and eyes forward the whole time, as if tracking an opponent.
Do 4 lengths at moderate pace, then 4 lengths as fast as you can without crossing.
If your feet cross, slow down: speed without form is just bad habits faster.
coaching_points: Lateral movement escapes straight punches and sets up angles
Crossed feet mean one trip away from the canvas
Stay low — standing tall to move fast is a contradiction

title: In-and-Out Jab Round
instructions: Start out of range from a heavy bag or imaginary opponent.
Step-drag in and land the jab as your lead foot plants; immediately step straight back out.
Stay on the balls of your feet through the whole round — no flat-footed resting.
Vary the rhythm: sometimes double-step in, sometimes feint the entry and stay out.
Work 3 minutes, resting only in your stance, never by standing up.
Final 30 seconds: every entry must end with the jab landing — no empty steps.
coaching_points: In-and-out movement controls range; range controls the fight
The exit is as important as the entry — don't admire your jab
Light feet, not fast feet: efficiency beats frantic bouncing

title: Circle the Heavy Bag
instructions: Take jab range from the heavy bag.
Circle the bag to your left for 90 seconds using small step-drag steps, maintaining exact range.
Reverse and circle right for 90 seconds — both directions must feel equal.
Throw a jab every third step without breaking stride or changing range.
If you drift too close or too far, correct with one small step — never a lunge.
Finish with 1 minute of circling where a partner randomly calls 'in!' and you step in with a 1-2, then resume range.
coaching_points: Circling at constant range is ring generalship in its simplest form
Small steps keep your weight under you; lunges hand your balance to the opponent
Move your feet as much when you're 'doing nothing' as when attacking

title: L-Step Angle Creation
instructions: Face an imaginary opponent in your stance.
Step your lead foot out at a 45-degree angle to the side (forming the foot of the 'L'), then drag the rear foot to reset.
You should now be offline from where the opponent's straight punches travel, but still in range to punch.
Throw a 1-2 from the new angle, then L-step back to center.
Practice both sides for 2 minutes, then add a pivot after the L-step for sharper angles.
Never step straight back to escape — the L-step replaces the backward retreat.
coaching_points: Angles make you hard to hit and easy to hit from — it's pure profit
Stepping straight back keeps you in the line of fire; stepping offline ends the exchange on your terms
Land in a stance after every L-step, ready to punch immediately

title: Combination Then Exit Angle
instructions: On the heavy bag, throw a 1-2-3 combination.
The instant the hook lands, pivot or L-step out to an angle — don't stand in front of the bag.
Reset at the new angle, throw the combination again, exit the other way.
Work 3 minutes; every combination must end with an exit step, no exceptions.
Round two: after the exit, immediately throw a counter 1-2 from the angle before resetting.
If you catch yourself backing straight up, stop the round and restart it.
coaching_points: Finishing a combination in front of your opponent is volunteering for the counter
The exit step is part of the combination — drill it like one
Angles after punching turn defense into your next offense

title: Cut the Ring (Partner)
instructions: You and a partner move in an open space; the partner tries to circle away, you try to stay in front of them.
Use small step-drag steps to cut off their escape — step to where they're going, not where they are.
Never lunge or chase with big steps; if you lunge, the partner gets a free pass for 10 seconds.
Keep your guard up and stay in stance the whole time — you're hunting, not running.
Switch roles every 2 minutes for 3 rounds each.
The goal is to corner the partner using footwork alone, no punches.
coaching_points: Cutting the ring is geometry: shrink their space with each step
Lunging after a mover wastes energy and leaves you off balance when they turn
Stay patient — the ring gets smaller on its own if your steps are disciplined

title: Slip Rope Weave
instructions: Tie a rope (or hand wraps knotted together) between two points at about shoulder height.
Stand at one end in your stance; roll under the rope by bending your knees and dipping your head to the side.
Come back up on the other side with your hands still at your cheeks.
Walk the length of the rope, rolling under it every step — down on one side, up on the other.
Add a jab before each roll: jab, roll under, come up, jab again.
Work the rope for 3 minutes; your legs should burn — that's the point.
coaching_points: Rolls come from the knees, not from bending at the waist
Hands stay home through the entire roll — dropping them is the classic error
Moving head + moving feet together is what makes defense real

title: Mirror Slip Technique Check
instructions: Face a mirror in your stance.
Slip to your left: shift your head about 6 inches off center, bending slightly at the knees and waist together.
Return to center, then slip right the same way. Watch that your eyes stay level — no dipping or rising.
Add variety: slip left, slip right, roll under — never the same move twice in a row.
Do 2 minutes slow and precise, then 1 minute at speed while keeping the movement small.
If your head moves more than a few inches, you're over-slipping and wasting motion.
coaching_points: A slip moves the head just off the punch's path — inches, not feet
Predictable head movement (same rhythm every time) gets timed and punished
Weight stays centered; reaching with the slip is just falling with style

title: Jab, Slip, Cross
instructions: Shadowbox the sequence: throw the jab, slip outside (to your left for orthodox), then throw the cross.
The slip must come from a small knee bend and torso shift — your head goes offline while your feet stay planted.
Return from the slip directly into the cross; the rotation of the slip loads the cross.
Do 2 minutes slow, grooving the rhythm: punch — move — punch.
Next 2 minutes: alternate slipping inside and outside after the jab, cross follows each.
Final minute at full speed — the slip must stay small even when you're moving fast.
coaching_points: Defense between punches is what separates combinations from arm-flailing
The slip loads your hips for the cross — defense becomes offense
Keep the rear hand on your cheek through the slip; it's your insurance

title: Controlled Pull Counter
instructions: In your stance, practice the pull: shift your weight onto your rear foot, letting your head drift back just out of range.
The movement is small — a few inches — chin tucked, eyes forward, guard intact.
The instant your weight settles back, fire the cross counter off the rear foot.
Do 10 slow reps in the mirror, checking that you never lean past your balance point.
With a partner throwing slow jabs, pull and counter for 2-minute rounds.
If you feel yourself falling backward, the pull is too big — shrink it.
coaching_points: The pull is a weight shift, not a lean — leaning back is a balance disaster
Counter immediately; a pull without a counter is just retreating
This is an advanced timing move — master the slip first

title: Roll Under the Hook
instructions: A partner throws slow lead hooks at your head (gloves on, controlled).
As the hook comes, bend your knees and roll your head under and slightly to the side of the punch.
Your hands stay at your cheeks through the entire roll.
Come up on the other side already punching — the roll ends in your counter.
Start at quarter speed for 2 minutes, then half speed; never go full speed in this drill.
Switch sides so you practice rolling both directions.
coaching_points: Roll under hooks, never straight punches — rolling into a cross is a classic knockout
Don't roll too low; stay coiled and ready to spring up punching
The counter is the point of the roll — defense that doesn't lead to offense is just surviving

title: Static Balance Block Test
instructions: Take your stance; a partner faces you wearing gloves.
The partner throws one slow punch at a time — first open-hand taps to your shoulders, then light straight punches.
Block each one from your stance: gloves to the head shots, elbows to the body shots.
The goal is balance, not speed — don't get pushed over, don't step, don't lean.
Start with one punch every 5 seconds; as you stabilize, go to one every 3 seconds.
Harder version: throw any punch and hold it out while the partner taps your exposed side — stay rooted.
coaching_points: This tests whether you can stand properly before it tests your defense
Block by recovering your gloves to position, not by chasing the punch
Exhale sharply on each block — breath and a slight brace repel the impact

title: Outside Parry Against the Jab
instructions: A partner throws slow, steady jabs at your head.
With your lead hand, tap the jab slightly aside — a small redirect, not a slap.
The motion is inches: deflect the punch off its line while your rear hand stays glued to your cheek.
Parry and immediately return the lead hand to guard — don't leave it hanging out.
Do 2 minutes parrying only, then 2 minutes where you parry and fire an immediate jab back.
Keep the parry minimal; big parries open your guard wider than the punch would have.
coaching_points: Parries work best against long straight punches — that's their designed purpose
Small deflection, instant return — the parry is a detour, not a destination
Chin stays down through the parry; lifting it to watch is a common mistake

title: High Guard Catch Round
instructions: Take a tight high guard: gloves at your forehead, elbows in, chin down, eyes open.
A partner throws slow 1-2 combinations at your head; catch them on your gloves and forearms.
Don't flinch, don't look away, don't hold your breath — absorb calmly.
Between combinations, the partner feints — don't react to feints, only to real punches.
Work 2-minute rounds; the partner gradually increases speed as your composure holds.
Final round: after each caught combination, fire back a 1-2 of your own.
coaching_points: Blocking is the easiest defense to learn — master it before fancy head movement
Eyes open and breathing: panic is what makes people turn away
A caught punch is a counter opportunity — the partner's hands are busy

title: Floor-to-Ceiling Bag Defense
instructions: Stand in front of a floor-to-ceiling (double-end style rebound) bag.
Throw a single jab; the bag rebounds toward your face — slip, parry, or block it.
You may not throw your next punch until you've defended the rebound.
Start with single punches, then build to 1-2s, defending after every combination.
The bag's return is unpredictable — that's the point; react, don't anticipate.
Work 3-minute rounds; count how many rebounds touch you and drive the number down.
coaching_points: This bag teaches the punch-defense-punch rhythm that defines real exchanges
Defend first, punch second — reversing that order is how you get caught
Keep the defensive motion small; the bag is fast and big motions won't catch up

title: Defense-Only Sparring Round
instructions: Light, controlled partner work: the partner attacks at about half speed and power.
You may not throw a single punch — only block, parry, slip, roll, and move your feet.
Survive 2-minute rounds purely on defense, staying calm and balanced.
Focus on one defensive tool per round: round one blocks only, round two slips and rolls, round three anything.
The partner should tell you afterward which defense you relied on most and which felt shakiest.
Build to 3-minute rounds; composure under fire is the skill being trained.
coaching_points: Removing offense forces your defense to actually work — no hiding behind punching
Stay relaxed; tension slows every defensive reaction
Footwork is defense too — stepping out of range counts and it's often the best option

title: Block-to-Counter on the Mitts
instructions: A partner holds mitts and feeds you slow jab-cross combinations.
Block or parry each punch, then fire the immediate counter the mitt holder presents.
The counter must come instantly — defense and offense are one beat, not two.
Start with scripted counters (block jab, counter cross), then let the holder call them live.
Work 3-minute rounds; the holder increases speed as your counters stay sharp.
Every defensive motion should load the counter: the block's rotation feeds the punch.
coaching_points: A defense that doesn't create offense is just delaying the inevitable
The fastest counter is the one your defensive motion already started
Stay in range through the defense — running away wastes the opening you earned

title: Shoulder Roll Introduction (Advanced)
instructions: Note: this is an advanced technique for experienced boxers — master the basic guard first.
In your stance, raise your lead shoulder high, tuck your chin behind it, rear hand at your cheek.
Practice the rolling motion slowly in a mirror: rotate the shoulder to deflect an imaginary straight punch.
The punch should glance off the deltoid, not land flush — angle, not absorption.
Have a partner throw very slow straight punches while you roll them off the shoulder.
Never use this at close range or against hooks until a coach clears you — it has real limitations.
coaching_points: The shoulder roll suits certain body types and styles — it's not for everyone
It fails against tight hooks and at clinch range; know its limits
Hands stay free to counter — that's the technique's entire payoff

title: 1-2 Metronome (Heavy Bag)
instructions: Work the heavy bag for a 3-minute round throwing nothing but the jab-cross.
Keep an even rhythm — like a metronome — with full snap and full return on every punch.
Every jab sets up the cross; every cross is thrown with hip rotation and a pivoted rear foot.
Between combinations, bounce lightly in your stance — never flat-footed, never admiring the bag.
Round two: vary the rhythm — double up the jab sometimes (1-1-2), pause sometimes — but only 1s and 2s.
Count your clean 1-2s per round; the number should rise as the motion gets automatic.
coaching_points: The 1-2 is the foundation every longer combination is built from — it must be automatic
Even rhythm first, broken rhythm later; chaos without fundamentals is just flailing
Both punches return to guard — the combination isn't done until the hands are home

title: 1-2-3 Builder (Heavy Bag)
instructions: On the heavy bag, throw the 1-2, then add the lead hook: jab-cross-hook.
The hook pivots the lead foot with a 90-degree elbow — the same geometry from the mirror drill.
Throw the three punches as one flowing motion, not three separate punches.
After the hook, snap back to guard before anything else.
Work 3 minutes, then add a final cross: 1-2-3-2 for the last minute of each round.
If the hook gets loopy when you're tired, slow down — the arc must stay tight.
coaching_points: Straight punches then a hook is the classic head-target combination — learn its feel
The hook's rotation is the same hip turn as the cross, just redirected
Flow matters more than power; speed comes from relaxation between punches

title: Head-Body Level Change (Heavy Bag)
instructions: On the heavy bag, throw a 1-2 to the head, then drop your level and throw a 1-2 to the body.
The level change comes from bending your knees — never from reaching down or bowing at the waist.
Alternate head and body every combination for the full round.
Keep your eyes up and chin tucked even when punching low — the head stays protected.
Round two: mix it — 1-2 head then hook to the body, or double jab body then cross head.
Finish each round with 30 seconds of free head-body mixing at speed.
coaching_points: Body punches make opponents drop their hands — then the head is open
Bend the knees to change levels; the spine angle barely changes
Never admire body work with your head down — come back up behind your guard

title: Jab to Body, Cross to Head
instructions: Step in with a level change and drive the jab into the bag's midsection.
Come up off the jab and fire the cross to the head in one continuous motion.
The combination is down-up: body shot drops the guard, head shot exploits it.
Keep the rear hand at your cheek during the body jab — you're bent, not open.
Work 3 minutes alternating with the reverse: jab head, cross body.
Add footwork in round three: step in with the combo, pivot out after.
coaching_points: High-low combinations are among the highest-percentage sequences in boxing
The level change must be quick — lingering low is dangerous
Sell the body shot with your knees so the head shot lands clean

title: Combination Exit Jab (Mitts)
instructions: A partner holds mitts; throw any 3-punch combination they call.
The instant the last punch lands, throw an exit jab while stepping out at an angle.
The exit jab doesn't need power — its job is to cover your exit and reset range.
Never finish a combination standing in the pocket; the exit is mandatory.
The holder occasionally throws a counter mitt at you after your combo — the exit jab must beat it.
Work 3-minute rounds, varying the combinations; the exit stays constant.
coaching_points: Most beginners get hit after their own combinations, not during them
The exit jab buys safe distance while keeping you offensively engaged
Angle out, never straight back — the footwork drills built this habit

title: Championship Rounds (Heavy Bag)
instructions: Three 3-minute heavy bag rounds with 1-minute rests — full fight simulation.
Combinations only: no single punches allowed for the entire drill.
Pace yourself like a real fight: busy first round, measured second, everything left in the third.
In the last 30 seconds of each round, empty the tank — then check: is your guard still up?
Between rounds, hands stay up while you breathe; dropping them in the rest is a habit, not recovery.
Score each round: clean combinations landed vs. times your guard dropped from fatigue.
coaching_points: Technique under fatigue is the real test — anyone looks good fresh
The guard must survive the round, not just start it
Pace with your breathing: exhale on every punch, never hold your breath in a flurry

title: Jump Rope Rounds
instructions: Jump rope for 3-minute rounds with 1-minute rests, matching boxing round timing.
Stay on the balls of your feet with small, quiet jumps — barely leaving the ground.
Keep your shoulders relaxed and turn the rope with your wrists, not your arms.
Alternate 1 minute basic bounce, 1 minute boxer's step (shifting weight side to side), 1 minute high knees.
Build from 3 rounds to 6 over several weeks.
If you trip, restart the jump immediately — recovering rhythm fast is part of the training.
coaching_points: Rope work builds the calf endurance and rhythm that footwork runs on
Relaxed shoulders: tension in the rope becomes tension in your punches
Boxing conditioning is interval-based — train in rounds, not in miles

title: Heavy Bag Sprint Intervals
instructions: Set an interval timer: 20 seconds all-out, 40 seconds easy, for 8 cycles.
During the 20-second bursts, throw non-stop flurries at the heavy bag — maximum output.
During the 40-second recovery, bounce lightly in your stance and breathe — hands stay up.
Keep punching form honest during the bursts; sloppy tired punches injure wrists.
Rest 2 minutes, then do a second block of 8 if your form survived the first.
Track your punch count per burst; the goal is maintaining output across all 8.
coaching_points: Fights are won in bursts — train the burst and the recovery between them
The easy intervals are active: stance, bounce, breathe, guard up
If your output collapses by round 5, your pacing needs work, not just your fitness

title: Fartlek Roadwork
instructions: Run for 30 minutes total on a route with some variation (hills ideal, flat fine).
Alternate 2 minutes easy jogging with 1 minute of hard pickups — sprint the pickups.
During easy sections, practice boxing breathing: rhythmic exhales, relaxed shoulders.
During pickups, drive with your arms as if pumping punches — running form feeds fighting form.
Finish the last 5 minutes with 30-second sprint / 30-second jog alternations.
Cool down with 5 minutes of walking; stretch at the gym, not immediately after.
coaching_points: Boxing is an interval sport — fartlek running matches its energy demands better than steady jogging
Keep roadwork moderate in volume; excessive long slow distance can blunt punching power
Consistency beats heroics: regular 30-minute sessions over occasional epics

title: Technique Under Fatigue
instructions: Do a hard conditioning burst first: 2 minutes of burpees, mountain climbers, or all-out bag flurries.
Immediately — no rest — shadowbox for 2 minutes focusing purely on technique.
Throw clean 1-2s, hooks with proper rotation, and keep your guard perfect despite the fatigue.
Have a partner (or camera) watch specifically for: dropping hands, arm punches, and stance widening.
Rest 1 minute, then repeat the whole sequence twice more.
The drill is passed when your third-round technique looks like your first.
coaching_points: Fights are decided late when technique degrades — this trains technique to survive
Fatigue exposes your true habits; whatever breaks here is what needs drilling fresh
Slow down before you get sloppy — clean slow beats fast and broken
